To obsess means to think about something — or someone — so constantly, so intensely, and so uncontrollably that it takes over your mind. The defining feature isn't just that you think about something a lot. It's that you can't stop, even when you try. The thought keeps returning on its own.
What Makes It Different from Simply "Thinking About Something"

Consider this scale:

Think about → Care about → Love → Be passionate about → Obsess

Each step is more intense than the last. "Obsess" sits at the extreme end. When you obsess over something, the thought doesn't stay neatly in its place — it bleeds into everything else. You're at dinner, but your mind is on that thing. You're trying to sleep, but that thought won't leave. That inability to switch off is the heart of the word.

1. Someone obsesses over / about something

This is the active form. The person is the one whose mind has been taken over.

  • She obsesses over every tiny detail of her work.
  • He obsesses about what people think of him.
  • They obsess over money constantly.

"Over" and "about" are both correct here and nearly interchangeable. "Over" feels slightly more intense in most contexts; "about" feels a bit more casual — but both work fine.

2. Someone is obsessed with / by something (most common)

This is the passive form, and it's the most frequently used construction in everyday English.

  • She is obsessed with true crime podcasts.
  • He was obsessed with becoming the best in his field.
  • They are completely obsessed by the idea of moving abroad.

"Obsessed with" is far more common in casual speech. "Obsessed by" has a slightly more formal or literary flavor but means the same thing. Both are correct.

3. Something obsesses someone (less common, but correct)

Here, the thing is the subject — it's doing the obsessing to the person. You'll see this more in writing than in speech.

  • The unanswered question obsessed him for years.
  • Fear of failure obsesses her.
  • One image from that day obsessed the artist throughout his life.

This pattern emphasizes that the person has no control — the thought acts upon them, rather than the other way around.
The Tone: Negative, Neutral, or Positive?

Traditionally, "obsess" carries a slightly negative or cautionary weight. It suggests that something is occupying more mental space than it should — often to the point of being unhealthy, harmful to relationships, or interfering with normal life.

  • He was so obsessed with his career that he ignored his family.
  • Her obsession with perfection made her miserable.

In modern informal usage, however — especially in conversation and on social media — "obsess" and "obsessed" are frequently used in a purely enthusiastic, positive way. The "can't stop thinking about it" quality remains, but the negative edge is dropped.

  • I am completely obsessed with this new café.
  • She's been obsessing over that album all week. (= she loves it and can't stop listening)
  • We are obsessed — this show is incredible.

Context will almost always make the meaning clear.
The Important Nuance: It Implies a Lack of Control

This is what separates obsess from words like love, enjoy, or even be passionate about. When you are passionate about something, you are in control — you choose to dedicate energy to it. When you obsess, the thought has power over you. It demands your attention whether or not you give it permission.

This is also why "obsess" is used in psychology to describe intrusive, unwanted thought patterns. The clinical condition OCD (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder) gets its name from this same root idea.

• Think about → neutral, no intensity, fully in control
  • Worry about → negative focus, but manageable
  • Be passionate about → positive and controlled dedication
  • Be fixated on → close to "obsess," but more clinical and detached in tone
  • Obsess → extreme, persistent, uncontrollable — can be joyfully positive (informal) or seriously negative depending on context
A Few Natural Examples Across Different Contexts

• Stop obsessing over things you can't control. (advice to let go)
  • She has been obsessed with astronomy since she was twelve. (a deep, long-standing passion)
  • He obsessed about the argument for days, replaying every word. (anxious, unwanted rumination)
  • The whole team is obsessed with winning this year. (intense focus — could be admirable or excessive)
  • I'm obsessed with this recipe, I've made it five times this month. (casual, enthusiastic love)
To obsess is to be held captive by a thought or feeling — to think about something so relentlessly and uncontrollably that it dominates your mind, whether you want it to or not.
